newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister fears catastrophe over weak army.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister fears catastrophe over weak army.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, firing a new shot in a battle for more army funding, said on Tuesday Russia faced a catastrophe unless it took extreme measures to reform the army.

"The armed forces today have come to the point where a further reduction in their combat readiness could lead to unforeseeble, tragic consequences," Rodionov told a meeting of the military top brass in Moscow.
"If extreme measures are not taken to reform the army in the near future, the consequences for the state could be catastrophic."

Rodionov's comments, in television footage shot by NTV commercial television, stepped up his struggle to persuade the government to increase defence spending and pay soldiers who have not received their wages for months.
He has played down talk of a military rebellion but said repeatedly that the problems could soon get out of control unless defence spending is increased.

In a sign of top-level concern, President Boris Yeltsin discussed the state of the armed forces with Prime Minister Viktor Cheromyrdin in a telephone converstaion on Tuesday from the clinic where he is recovering after heart surgery.
A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin had specifically asked Chernomyrdin whether wages had been paid, as promised, to the armed forces.

The military meeting was attended by Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, who sat expressionless through Rodionov's brief introductory speech. Chernomyrdin was due to discuss the reforms with defence officials later on Tuesday.
Rodionov has been pushing for better funding and reforms, including reducing the size the army, since he was appointed by Yeltsin on July 17.
But difficulties have mounted since then because many servicemen have not been paid for months. The failure if Russian troops to crush separatists in Chechnya has also sapped morale.
Rodionov said Russia could be caught unprepared if global or regional tensions worsened and threatened its security.
"The deepening economic crisis in the country, social instability, the lack of unity in society...have pushed problems of the combat readiness of the armed forces to the extreme," Rodionov said.
The armed forces were long the pride of the Soviet Union but funding has been slashed since the superpower broke up in 1991.

A leaked report by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIS) last month said controls had weakened over the nuclear arsenal. Russian media reports say suicide and robberies are on the increase in the army.
In a sign of confusion, a Kremlin official said this month that even people at the helm of military reforms have only a vague idea of the size of the country's armed forces.

The London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies Russia has about 1.27 million active members of the armed forces. Yuri Baturin, head of the advisory Defence Council, said the figure could be as high as 2.5 million.

The liberal newspaper Sevodnya said on Tuesday that Baturin and Rodionov had clashed at a meeting on Monday over the military doctrine. It said Baturin wanted major changes but Rodionov had suggested that major surgery was not needed.

A confrontation over the military doctrine would create a serious obstacle to army reforms. Most defence analysts say serious reform cannot start until a new doctrine is worked out to replace the one dating from 1993.
